title: Discovery and development, 1860–75: Lister and Pasteur

review.note: Original content following 4HI1 Breadth study B2, key topic 2.

learn.intro: Pasteur's germ theory transformed understanding of disease. Lister used it to fight infection in surgery, Parliament passed a compulsory Public Health Act, and Elizabeth Garrett broke into the male world of medicine.

blocks.p: Louis Pasteur, a French chemist, was asked to find out why wine and beer went sour. He showed that microbes (germs) in the air caused decay. In 1861, using swan-necked flasks, he showed that liquid stayed fresh when microbes from the air could not reach it — disproving spontaneous generation.

Effects: germ theory showed that microbes cause decay and, as later work proved, disease. It gave a scientific reason for cleanliness, led to antiseptics in surgery, and made identifying specific germs and developing vaccines possible. Many doctors were slow to accept it.

sections.title: 2. Lister and antiseptics

blocks.p: Joseph Lister, a surgeon in Glasgow, read Pasteur's work and thought germs might cause infection in wounds. In 1865 he used carbolic acid on the wound of an 11-year-old boy, James Greenlees, who had a compound fracture; the wound healed without infection.

Lister soaked dressings and instruments in carbolic acid and sprayed it in the air during operations. He published his results in 1867: death rates in his operations fell sharply. There was opposition: carbolic acid irritated skin, the methods slowed operations, and many surgeons did not accept germ theory.

evidence: 1865: Lister treats James Greenlees with carbolic acid.

sections.title: 3. The Public Health Act 1875

blocks.p: By the 1870s attitudes were changing: working men in towns had the vote from 1867, so politicians needed their support; germ theory and Snow's work showed the link between dirt and disease; and Bazalgette's new London sewers (built after the 'Great Stink' of 1858) showed what could be done.

The Public Health Act of 1875 was compulsory. Councils had to provide clean water, remove sewage, and appoint a Medical Officer of Health and sanitary inspectors. It marked the end of laissez-faire in public health.

evidence: 1867: more working men get the vote.

sections.title: 4. Hospitals, nursing and women in medicine

blocks.p: Nightingale's influence continued: trained nurses spread, and new hospitals used her pavilion design with light, airy, easily cleaned wards.

Elizabeth Garrett was refused entry to medical schools because she was a woman. She found a loophole: the Society of Apothecaries had not banned women, and in 1865 she gained its licence, becoming the first woman to qualify in Britain. She opened a dispensary for women in London and later gained a medical degree in Paris (1870). The Medical Act of 1876 allowed women to qualify as doctors.

evidence: 1865: Garrett qualifies through the Society of Apothecaries.

misconceptions.right: Many surgeons resisted: carbolic was unpleasant and germ theory was doubted.

misconceptions.wrong: Pasteur proved germs caused human disease in 1861.
misconceptions.right: He showed microbes caused decay; the link to specific diseases was proved later, especially by Koch.
